lines.text: program and has been theorized to capture the peak response
in areas of concern where resonant WIO may occur [1]-[4].
The impact of atmospheric turbulence and wind profile has
historically been considered of secondary importance to
aeroelastic scaling and Reynolds number matching. Efforts
were made in the 1960s to replicate the ground-wind profile
in TDT; however, these were unsuccessful and were not
further pursued at the time [1], [2].
Atmospheric-boundary-layer (ABL) test techniques have
since been developed for other wind-tunnel facilities to
replicate ground-wind profiles for analysis of many civil
engineering structures. Successful experimental techniques
have been demonstrated to reasonably represent wind-profile
shape and turbulence content [5]-[7]. ABL simulation is
typically achieved with the insertion of angled spires far
upstream of the test article, with roughness elements installed
along the floor between the spires and test article as detailed
in References [5]-[7]. All ABL-simulation wind tunnels
known to the authors at the time of this publication are low-
speed, ambient-pressure wind tunnels with air as the test
medium. In ambient-pressure air, the Reynolds number will
be mismatched by a factor approximately equal to the
geometric scale of the model. Therefore, successful
simulation of the ABL in the Reynolds number regime of
interest for launch vehicles has never been achieved in these
wind tunnels. Additionally, with air as the test medium at
fixed pressure, it would be extremely difficult to construct an
aeroelastically-scaled model of a large launch vehicle for use
in any ABL wind tunnel due to the scaling limitations
detailed in Reference [8]. For dynamic aeroelastic models,
these scaling parameters include mass ratio and reduced
frequency, in addition to the replication of mode shapes and
structural damping [8].
The purpose of the research effort described in this paper is
to evaluate the effect of an ABL upon the WIO response of
launch vehicles and to create a database for community use.
Aeroelastically-scaled models of representative vehicles
were constructed and were tested at flight-representative
Reynolds numbers.
2. TEST DESCRIPTION
Wind-Tunnel Facility
The TDT is a large, variable pressure, transonic wind tunnel
that is uniquely designed to accommodate testing of
aeroelastic models. It is a continuous-flow, single-return,
slotted-test-section wind tunnel capable of testing at total
pressures from 0.005 to 1.0 atmospheres, over a Mach
number range from near zero to 1.20 using either air or heavy
gas (R-134a) as the test medium. The test section of the TDT
is 16 feet by 16 feet square with cropped corners, yielding a
cross-sectional area of 248 square feet. The TDT utilizes a
number of model support systems, including a variety of
sidewall and sting support systems, a cable-mount system,
and a floor turntable where GWL models are mounted to
allow for variation in wind azimuth angle. A sketch of the
TDT is shown in Figure 1, with cutaways revealing some key
features of the wind tunnel. One of these key features are the
bypass valves that enable rapid flow-speed reduction when
models encounter an instability. Additionally, a model catch
screen protects the main drive fan blades in the event of a
catastrophic model failure.
Unlike typical wind-tunnel testing, which focuses upon
modeling the aerodynamics experienced by a flight vehicle,
the study of aeroelasticity requires modeling of the structural
response of the flight vehicle when exposed to representative
aerodynamics. Typically regarded as the world’s premier
aeroelastic test facility [9]-[12], the TDT fulfills a unique
niche in the wind-tunnel infrastructure as a result of its
unparalleled ability to manipulate fluid-structure scaling
parameters.
Figure 1. Sketch of the Transonic Dynamics Tunnel with
cutaways revealing key features
Data Acquisition
Data records were sampled at 10 kHz. Signal conditioning
provided by a Precision Filters Inc. (PFI) system filtered all
analog channels with a low-pass, 4-pole, pulse-mode (LP4P)
filter with a cutoff frequency of 3 kHz. The pulse-mode
setting is similar to a Bessel filter with slightly better roll-off
characteristics and is a good choice for time domain
applications, including time domain waveform analysis.
Data record length was 8.7 seconds for acquisition of flow
survey rake data and 15 seconds for acquisition of launch
vehicle WIO data. Channel statistics for the flow survey rake
parameters stabilized after approximately five seconds of
data, and increased sample time did not change the results
significantly. Therefore 8.7 seconds is likely adequate to
characterize the flow and was chosen to align data with a
customer data system [13]. WIO data, on the other hand, is
rather nonstationary. Post-test analysis of data records have
revealed that time history amplitudes of the primary mode of
interest (frequency of 30 Hz) were continually increasing or
decreasing for the duration of the 15-second data record in
some rare cases. Therefore, the nonstationarity of WIO
behavior may impact some results and has not been fully
assessed at the writing of this paper.
